summary: No single body tracks AI adoption across America's hundreds of thousands of congregations - coverage comes from research firms, faith-tech platforms, and academic institutes, and this page names them rather than pretending a census exists. Sermon research, translation, accessibility, and administration are the working uses; every tradition is writing its own guidance.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey puts the latest AI adoption figure for NAICS 81, other services, a category that includes religious organizations, at 13.7%, up from 12.6% in the prior period. That is the only official measured adoption number available, and it covers a much broader set of firms than churches alone, so it should be read as a ceiling rather than a precise count of congregations using AI. No better government measure exists yet for the sector specifically.

What deployment looks like inside faith organizations is clearest from Gloo, the sector's main technology platform, used by thousands of US churches according to this site's curated points. Gloo describes AI as a foundational capability across its platform for mission effectiveness, preserving relational ministry, and creating practical value. Its AI Studio offers developers API-first support for inference, retrieval augmented generation, and assistant workflows, with values-aligned models and trusted content as the selling point. That suggests the practical uses concentrate in back-office and content workflows rather than replacing pastoral presence.

The ethics conversation is well developed even where the adoption data is thin. AI and Faith, an interfaith nonprofit, frames the core issues as control and power, privacy, bias and discrimination, economic well-being, and what it means to be human, and notes that 85 percent of the world's population claims a religious affiliation, making these questions spiritual as well as moral for most people. The University of Notre Dame's Institute for Ethics and the Common Good works on human formation in the AI transition, with its director Meghan Sullivan observing that many industry workers talk very flippantly about job displacement, while faculty fellow Lily Abadal notes that AI awareness among Catholic school and ministry leaders has been evolving.

The research base beyond the Census is fragmented. Barna Group's State of the Church work quantitatively tracks AI adoption, perception, and use among US congregations and ministry leaders, per this site's curated points, and the Hartford Institute for Religion Research has a 45 year history of surveying congregational life and digital adoption. Pew Research Center's religion work periodically measures public and clergy attitudes toward technology, though the excerpts harvested here do not surface specific AI findings from any of these three organizations.

A reader deciding whether to deploy should take two things from the available material. First, the sector now has dedicated infrastructure, in Gloo, and dedicated ethics networks, in AI and Faith and Notre Dame, so a congregation does not have to improvise from generic enterprise tools. Second, the official measurement remains coarse, and the survey organizations that could say more about actual congregational use have not yet published AI-specific numbers in the material reviewed here. The prudent posture is to treat 13.7% as a broad service-sector benchmark, not a church-specific adoption rate, and to look to Gloo's tooling and the ethics networks for guidance on what values-aligned deployment looks like in practice.

https://ethics.nd.edu/.brief: The Notre Dame Institute for Ethics and the Common Good, directed by Meghan Sullivan, convenes a multidisciplinary community to tackle pressing ethical issues. It promotes interdisciplinary research, policy leadership, and practical models for ethical AI design, development, and deployment. The institute will host a second DELTA summit focused on human formation and dignity in the AI transition. Sullivan notes that many industry workers “talk very flippantly” about job displacement and AI’s speed and cost, while Lily Abadal observes that AI awareness is evolving.

https://www.barna.com/.brief: Barna Group, a Christian research organization, offers data and insights on faith, culture, and ministry trends. Their website hosts articles, reports, podcasts, courses, and services, including a free webcast replay that examines six trends shaping pastoral leadership. The site also promotes Barna’s latest research report, The State of Pastors, Volume 2, which explores how pastors navigate post-pandemic life and ministry across self-leadership, church leadership, and cultural leadership. A series of conversations features pastors Glenn Packiam, Rich Villodas, and Sharon Hodde Miller discussing leadership challenges and the health of the church. New Barna data indicates that one in three young adults is increasing church attendance, revealing who is leaning in and what they seek at church.

https://www.gloo.us/ai.brief: According to Gloo, its AI offering provides models, developer tools, and benchmarks that are aligned with the values of faith-based organizations. The company describes AI as a foundational capability across its platform, intended to support mission effectiveness, preserve relational ministry, and create practical value. Developers using Gloo AI Studio can access connected infrastructure including production environment tools, trusted content, and values-aligned models. The platform also offers API-first support for inference, RAG, and assistant workflows, with dynamic selection of the appropriate model for each request.

https://aiandfaith.org/.brief: AI and Faith is an organization that brings religious and faith-based perspectives to discussions about artificial intelligence ethics. The group argues that emerging AI issues—including control, privacy, bias, discrimination, and questions about human identity—are fundamentally moral questions, and that the world's religious traditions contain "ancient wisdom" relevant to how AI should be developed and used. The organization works to connect theologians, tech creators, researchers, and ethicists to integrate faith-based values into conversations about AI's ethical implications, aiming to introduce "humility and historicity into an industry that has often rejected them both."
